opus-5.5.text:
I think it's useful to separate the hype from where the dollars are actually flowing. If you talk to folks inside large pharma, the places they're getting real, measurable value from AI today are mostly not the headline-grabbing "AI designed a drug" stories. They're much more operational.

A big one is clinical development. Trials are the most expensive and slowest part of the whole enterprise, so anything that speeds up patient recruitment, site selection, protocol design, or regulatory document drafting translates directly into time and money. Language models are very good at the enormous amount of paperwork that surrounds a trial, things like clinical study reports, submissions, and safety narratives. That's unglamorous, but if you shave months off a program, that's worth a lot when every day of patent life matters.

The second area is the front end of discovery, where you see things like protein structure prediction, antibody and small molecule design, and property prediction. That's real and it's improving quickly, but I'd say the value there is still more about making individual steps more efficient than about fundamentally changing success rates. Most drugs still fail in the clinic because of biology. We picked the wrong target, or we don't understand the disease well enough, and better chemistry doesn't fix that.

That's actually what I find most exciting and what I think is still underexploited: using AI to model biology itself. We're getting to the point where we can generate perturbation data at massive scale, like knocking out or turning on genes across millions of cells, and train models that start to predict how cells respond. If we can build something like a virtual cell, then you can ask much better questions about which targets are worth pursuing before you spend a decade and a billion dollars finding out.

So my read is that pharma is capturing value today in efficiency, in documents, operations, and point solutions in chemistry. The bigger prize, which is improving the probability that a drug actually works, is going to come from better models of biology, and that's still early. The companies that figure out how to generate the right data to train those models are going to have a real advantage.

r002.rationale: It calls trials expensive and slow, but does not explain pharma budget holders’ interest by comparing development spending with discovery spending.

r003.rationale: It says many drugs fail in clinical trials because of biological uncertainty, but gives no roughly 10% industry probability of success.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think it's worth separating the hype from where the dollars are actually moving. If you look at where pharma is spending real money on AI today, it's mostly not in the glamorous part, the "design a novel drug from scratch" part. It's in the operational layers of the business. Clinical trial design, patient recruitment, site selection, regulatory document generation, pharmacovigilance, summarizing the enormous volume of literature and internal data they're sitting on. These are places where the technology works today, the ROI is measurable, and nobody has to bet the company on it.

And that makes sense if you think about the economics. A phase three trial can cost hundreds of millions of dollars. If you can shave six months off enrollment, or pick better sites, or write the regulatory submission faster, that's a very concrete win. It's boring, but boring is where the value is captured first.

The second place is in discovery, and here I'd say the honest answer is that it's still mostly in the "tooling" phase rather than the "transformation" phase. Structure prediction obviously changed the field. Generative models for small molecules and antibodies are genuinely useful for expanding and prioritizing the space you search. But the bottleneck in drug development was never really "can I come up with a molecule." The bottleneck is biology. Which target, in which patient, with what safety profile. Most drugs fail in the clinic because we picked the wrong hypothesis, not because the chemistry was bad. And AI has helped a lot less there so far, because the data you'd need to learn those things largely doesn't exist yet, or exists in fragmented, non-interoperable forms inside companies that don't share it.

So my interpretation is that pharma is extracting real value at the edges, in efficiency, and is still waiting for the core promise, which is better targets and higher clinical success rates. The companies that are thinking most clearly about it are the ones investing in generating the right data, not just buying models. Large scale perturbation data, patient-level longitudinal data, functional genomics at scale. Because the models are increasingly going to be commodity. The data and the biological hypotheses are not.

And one more thing I'd add. I think there's a cultural dimension. Big pharma is organized around a very linear pipeline, and AI works best when you can close loops quickly, design, test, learn, redesign. The organizations that will get the most out of this are the ones willing to restructure how they do science, not just bolt a model onto the existing process. That's hard, and it's why a lot of the most interesting work is happening in newer companies that were built around that loop from day one.

astra-6.text:
I think the clearest value today is in making existing workflows more efficient. Pharma companies have a lot of expensive decisions to make: which targets to pursue, which molecules to synthesize, which experiments to run. AI can help narrow those choices and get more information out of the data they already have.

But I’d distinguish that from changing the probability that a drug actually succeeds. You can design a molecule that binds a protein beautifully and still have the wrong hypothesis about what causes the disease. So making molecules is one part of the problem; understanding which biological intervention will help a patient is another.

To me, the bigger opportunity is connecting prediction with experimentation. Can you use a model to choose an experiment, learn from the result, and progressively build a better understanding of the biology? That’s where AI could move beyond saving time and start changing what we’re able to discover.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the clearest value today is in making existing workflows more efficient: finding promising molecules, prioritizing experiments, and helping teams make sense of large amounts of data. Those are concrete problems where you can ask whether AI saves time or improves the quality of a decision.

The bigger opportunity is changing what we can discover. Can we understand biology well enough to identify a new target, or design a therapy that we wouldn’t otherwise know how to make? That’s a much higher bar. A molecule looking promising computationally is only the beginning; you still have to show that it works in a biological system and ultimately helps a patient.

So I’d distinguish the value companies can capture immediately through efficiency from the longer-term value of making drug discovery more predictive. The real test is whether these tools lead to better medicines.
